conceptBreakdown.heading: 8.1 Preserved Specimens Collections
conceptBreakdown.title: 8.1 Preserved Specimens Collections
conceptBreakdown.content:
A. Herbarium:
A Herbarium is a repository of dried, pressed, mounted, and catalogued plant specimens arranged according to an accepted system of classification (e.g., Bentham and Hooker system).

• Standard Dimensions:
  - Herbarium Sheet Size: $29\text{ cm} \times 41.5\text{ cm}$ ($11.5\text{ inches} \times 16.5\text{ inches}$).
  - Herbarium Label Size: $7\text{ cm} \times 12\text{ cm}$, located on the Bottom Right Corner of the sheet.

• Mandatory Label Information:
  1. Date of collection.
  2. Place/locality of collection.
  3. English name.
  4. Local / Vernacular name.
  5. Botanical / Scientific name.
  6. Family name.
  7. Collector's name.

• CRITICAL NEST QUESTION TRAP: What information is NOT present on a Herbarium label?
  - Height of the plant is NOT recorded on the label.
  - Internal anatomical details or ecological conditions are also omitted from the standard label.

• Chemical Preservation: Sheets/specimens are treated with 0.1% Mercuric Chloride ($\text{HgCl}_2$) or sprayed with carbon disulfide/DDT to prevent fungal and insect pest attack.

B. Museums:
Repositories housing preserved animal and plant specimens for study and reference.
• Preservation Media: Specimens preserved in jars in chemical solutions (typically 10% Formalin [formaldehyde] or 70% Ethanol).
• Insect Boxes: Insects are preserved by collecting, killing in killing jars (using potassium cyanide/ether), and pinning through the thorax into insect boxes.
• Large Animals: Mammals and birds are stuffed and preserved (taxidermy).
• Skeleton Collections: Skeletal frameworks are prepared and catalogued.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 8.2 Living Collections
conceptBreakdown.title: 8.2 Living Collections
conceptBreakdown.content:
A. Botanical Gardens:
Ex-situ collections of living plants cultivated for scientific research, conservation, and education. Plants are tagged with their scientific name and family.

• Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (Richmond, UK): Contains the world's largest herbarium (>7 million specimens) and living collections.

• Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanical Garden (Howrah, Kolkata, India): Famous for The Great Banyan Tree (*Ficus benghalensis*), which is over 250 years old with >3,600 prop roots, lacking a main trunk.

• National Botanical Research Institute (NBRI): Located in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India.

B. Zoological Parks (Zoos):
Enclosed facilities where wild animals are maintained in simulated natural environments under human care for ex-situ conservation, behavioral research, and education.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 8.3 Literature Aids & Identification Tools
conceptBreakdown.title: 8.3 Literature Aids & Identification Tools
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
TAXONOMIC IDENTIFICATION KEYS
                                    │
                         [ Pair of Statements ] ──► COUPLET
                                    │
           ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
           ▼                                                 ▼
   [ Statement 1 ] ──► LEAD                           [ Statement 2 ] ──► LEAD
   (Accept or Reject)                                 (Accept or Reject)
conceptBreakdown.content:
A. Taxonomic Keys:
Analytical devices used to identify unknown plants or animals based on similarities and differences.
• Dichotomous Key: Based on a set of contrasting choices between two options.
• Couplet: A pair of contrasting statements in a key.
• Lead: Each individual statement within a couplet.
• Analytical Nature: Keys are strictly analytical in nature. Separate taxonomic keys are required for each distinct taxonomic category (e.g., separate keys for family, genus, and species identification).
• Types of Dichotomous Keys:
  - Indented Key (Yoked Key): Choices are indented by distance from the margin; matching choices are placed at equal indentations.
  - Bracketed Key: Choices are listed sequentially in numbered pairs using brackets, making them easier to read for long diagnostic sequences.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Specialized Taxonomic Literature
conceptBreakdown.title: Specialized Taxonomic Literature

                                     │
         ┌───────────────┬───────────┴───────────┬───────────────┐
         ▼               ▼                       ▼               ▼
       FLORA          MANUAL                  MONOGRAPH      CATALOGUE
 Provides habitat &   Provides identification  Provides info  Alphabetical list
 distribution info   keys/names in an area   on ONE TAXON   of all species
conceptBreakdown.content:
• Flora: A comprehensive text containing the actual account of habitat, distribution, and seasonal occurrence of plant species in a specific geographic area (e.g., Flora of British India by J.D. Hooker). It provides an index to the plant species of that region.

• Manuals: Practical handbooks providing detailed instructions and diagnostic information useful for the identification of names of species found in a given area.

• Monographs: Comprehensive scientific publications containing exhaustive taxonomic, evolutionary, and ecological information on ANY ONE TAXON (e.g., a monograph on the family Solanaceae or the genus Pinus).

• Catalogues: An alphabetical or systematic register listing all species recorded in a defined territory, often including full bibliographic citations and references.

Couplet = pair of statements; Lead = single statement.
Monograph = information on ANY ONE TAXON; Flora = habitat & distribution index.
